t: Nebuchadnezzar II had the gate built c. 569 BCE on the north side of Babylon and dedicated it to Ishtar; it opened onto the Processional Way used for the New Year procession of the gods.
Its bricks were pressed in moulds, fired, glazed in blue to imitate lapis lazuli and sealed with bitumen, and the façade carried rows of dragons, aurochs and lions.
The German excavation under Robert Koldewey sent most of the gate and the Processional Way's lions to Berlin, and Iraq has petitioned for its return, notably in 2002 and 2009.
dyk: Each of the lions along the Processional Way was made of forty-six moulded bricks in eleven rows, and of the 120 lion friezes on the street the German excavators took 118.
ev: Nebuchadnezzar II ordered the gate built on the north side of Babylon
Claudius Rich's topographical records of the ruins of Babylon, the first ever published, appeared
Robert Koldewey began his part in the excavation of Babylon
The excavation, which had uncovered 14 metres of the gate's foundation, came to an end
After the First World War ended, the smaller frontal gate was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin
A smaller reproduction of the gate, built under Saddam Hussein, was completed in Iraq
The government of Iraq petitioned Germany to return the gate, and petitioned again in 2009

f.made: Built on the orders of Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon, who dedicated it to the goddess Ishtar; its glazed bricks were pressed, fired and glazed by Babylonian brickmakers
f.form: A double gate of glazed brick, 15 metres high with foundations extending another 14 metres underground, faced in blue with low-relief dragons, aurochs and lions, and carrying a 60-line Akkadian cuneiform inscription
f.where: The site is at Babylon, near present-day Hillah in Iraq; the reconstructed smaller frontal gate stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, and panels are in many other museums
f.known: blue glazed bricks meant to represent lapis lazuli; reliefs of mušḫuššu dragons, aurochs and lions; the Processional Way and the New Year procession; Nebuchadnezzar's dedication inscription; its reconstruction in Berlin; the debate over its return to Iraq
